title: The Brother Who Signed the Papers

voiceProfile.pov: Close third-person alternating between Jayant (the elder brother who stayed) and Vivek (the younger brother who left)
voiceProfile.tense: Past tense, structured across three distinct rhythmic movements
voiceProfile.register: Grounded, legalistic, familial, emotionally fraught with decades of unspoken ledgers
voiceProfile.narratorDistance: Dual close third-person; giving equal, agonizing validity to both brothers' positions
distinctiveDevices: The language of Maharashtra Land Revenue code, non-encumbrance certificates, 7/12 extract extracts, and stamp duty papers contrasting with tactile memories of the family wada
The triple-rhythm layout mapping cleanly to three temporal movements: Act I: The Wada of 1938; Act II: The Sub-Registrar's Office at Swargate; Act III: The Tea Stall on Bajirao Road
Physical ledgers and prescription receipts accumulated over fourteen years of home medical care

protagonist1.name: Jayant Kulkarni
protagonist1.family: Elder son of late Shrikant Kulkarni (postal surveyor) and late Malati Kulkarni; husband to Rohini (high school Marathi teacher); father to Sanika (14)
protagonist1.education: M.Sc in Chemistry from Fergusson College, Pune; B.Ed
protagonist1.career: High school chemistry teacher at Bhave High School, Sadashiv Peth, Pune (20 years of service)
habits: Rides a 2004 Bajaj Chetak scooter that he kicks three times before starting
Keeps all medical receipts filed by year inside cardboard box files tied with pink tape
Wears spectacles with silver wireframes that he cleans with his shirt hem
protagonist1.beliefs: Believes family duty is not an investment with a return; it is a debt you repay with your life; believes staying where you were born is an act of moral gravity
protagonist1.fears: Fears being remembered as a fool who sacrificed his own daughter's education to wipe his bedridden mother's back while his brother became rich in Hyderabad
protagonist1.flaws: Nurses a quiet, martyred bitterness; uses his caregiving sacrifices as moral leverage to invalidate his brother's contributions
protagonist1.speechStyle: Formal Marathi and precise English; patient, quiet, refuses to raise his voice even when insulted
protagonist1.secrets: Kept a handwritten notebook listing every single rupee spent on his mother's dialysis, insulin, and diapers from 2011 to 2024: total ₹38,42,110
protagonist1.memories: His mother's fingers clutching his wrist during her last winter in the ground-floor room, whispering: 'Jayant, don't let this roof go to strangers.'

protagonist2.name: Vivek Kulkarni
protagonist2.family: Younger son; married to Anjali (product manager in fintech); father to twins (6); lives in Gachibowli, Hyderabad
protagonist2.education: B.Tech from COEP, Pune; MS in Computer Science from University of Texas, Austin
protagonist2.career: Co-founder of an AI-driven supply chain startup in Hyderabad; has raised Series A but facing a severe 6-month funding winter and payroll crunch
protagonist2.income: Paper net worth on equity, but personal bank liquidity down to ₹4,20,000; needs his ₹1.9 crore share of the sale to keep his company alive
habits: Checks company Slack notifications every ninety seconds
Drinks Americanos without sugar from insulated travel mugs
Touches the back of his neck when lying or hiding panic
protagonist2.beliefs: Believes ancestral nostalgia is a luxury that living people cannot afford; believes sent money is real love, not second-class love
protagonist2.fears: Fears total financial collapse, laying off twenty-two engineers who trusted him, and returning to Pune as a bankrupt failure
protagonist2.flaws: Assumes money solves everything; minimized his brother's physical caregiving burden because he wire-transferred ₹40,000 every month from the US and Hyderabad
protagonist2.speechStyle: Fast-paced, modern corporate idiom mixed with colloquial Marathi, defensive when challenged on family presence
protagonist2.secrets: Pledged his personal apartment in Hyderabad as collateral for his company's working capital loan three months ago without telling his wife
protagonist2.memories: Playing cricket in the wada courtyard with a tennis ball that always broke the ground-floor stained glass fanlights

theProperty.name: Kulkarni Wada
theProperty.location: Sadashiv Peth, Pune; 4,200 square feet plot with a 3-storey timber and stone structure built in 1938 by grandfather Dattatreya Kulkarni
theProperty.commercialReality: Offered ₹3.80 crore by a local redevelopment firm (Surya Developers) to demolish the structure and build a 6-storey residential apartment complex
theProperty.splitTerms: 50-50 share between Jayant and Vivek after taxes and registration expenses: ₹1.82 crore each

timeline.1986–2004: Childhood in the wada; grandfather dies; father dies in 2004; Vivek goes to college and then America; Jayant stays to look after mother
timeline.2011: Mother Malati suffers first stroke; bedridden for 13 years; Jayant and Rohini manage daily bedsores, medicines, hospitalizations; Vivek sends regular wire transfers
timeline.October 2024: Mother passes away quietly at age 79. The wada becomes completely silent.
timeline.January 2025: Vivek flies into Pune with the developer's memorandum of understanding. Jayant must sign the sale deed as co-owner.
timeline.Present Day (Morning to Afternoon): The appointment at the Sub-Registrar's Office, Swargate, Pune. 3 hours, 44 signatures, thumb impressions on green bond paper, and the final walk down Bajirao Road.

recurringMotifs: The green stamp-duty bond papers with violet government seals
The grandfather's carved Sagwan teak door with the heavy iron ring latch
The cardboard box file containing thirteen years of hospital discharge summaries
The biometric thumbprint scanner flashing red before accepting the ink
The two cutting chais ordered at the street corner after the ink has dried
prohibitions: Neither brother is evil; Vivek is not a greedy Silicon Valley caricature; Jayant is not a saint without bitterness
The financial distress of Vivek is real and terrifying; the physical labor of Jayant was grueling and unrewarded
No miraculous compromise where the wada is saved as a museum; economic reality is inescapable in urban India
The ending honors the grief of both brothers without sentimentality
